analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income tax with a flat tax, repeals the estate tax, and caps entitlement spending.
analysis.headline: The House Majority Leader's flat-tax bill, with 9 cosponsors, was referred to four committees and two subcommittees and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the entire federal income tax system with a single flat rate on wage income and business income, dropping from 20% to 17% after two years. It repeals the estate and gift tax, the alternative minimum tax, and every federal tax credit. It also locks in the tax cuts with a rule requiring a three-fifths vote to raise taxes, caps the growth of entitlement programs (excluding Social Security) with automatic across-the-board cuts, and requires a balanced budget by 2002.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest winners would have been high-income households: the new tax code taxes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, so interest, dividends, and capital gains would have become untaxed, and the estate tax would disappear entirely. Employers and business owners would have gained a flat 17–20% tax on business income with the corporate alternative minimum tax repealed, plus the freedom to withdraw surplus assets from company pension plans without the existing 20% excise tax. Middle-income wage families would have benefited from very large standard deductions ($21,400 for couples plus $5,000 per dependent).

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated income tax with a single 20% rate, dropping to 17% after 1997, applied to taxable income above a large standard deduction of $21,400 for joint filers and $10,700 for singles, plus $5,000 per dependent.
Repeals the estate and gift tax for deaths and gifts after December 31, 1995, eliminating federal taxation of inherited wealth.
Repeals the corporate income tax and the alternative minimum tax, replacing them with a flat 20% (later 17%) tax on business income after deducting wages and business inputs.
Repeals every federal tax credit, including the earned income tax credit for low-wage workers.
Caps total entitlement and mandatory spending growth (excluding Social Security) at inflation plus population growth through 2002, enforced by automatic cuts, with a balanced budget required by 2002.

analysis.who_pays: Low-income working families would have paid more: the bill repeals all tax credits, including the earned income tax credit, and taxes unemployment compensation. Entitlement beneficiaries would have faced automatic cuts to hold spending to the caps — up to 4% for Medicare providers, 2% for federal retirement and veterans' benefits, and 1% for programs like food stamps, Medicaid, and aid to families with dependent children. Workers would have lost pension protections: the bill repeals nondiscrimination and coverage rules for employer pension plans and lets employers pull excess pension assets out of plans without the excise tax. Government and nonprofit employees would have faced a new 20% tax on the value of employer-provided benefits like health insurance. The revenue lost from untaxed capital income and the estate tax repeal would have shifted the tax burden toward wage earners or forced deeper domestic cuts.

drawbacks.text: Taxable income would be defined as wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation only — leaving interest, dividends, and capital gains entirely untaxed — so the tax cut concentrates on households whose income comes from wealth rather than work.

Repealing all credits, including the earned income tax credit, would raise taxes on many low-income working families even as the standard deduction rises, and unemployment compensation would remain taxable.

The bill repeals pension nondiscrimination, coverage, and top-heavy rules and allows employers to withdraw excess assets from defined-benefit pension plans without the 20% excise tax, removing protections for rank-and-file workers' retirement security.

Spending caps enforced by automatic sequestration would cut Medicare payments by up to 4%, federal retirement and veterans' benefits by up to 2%, and low-income programs such as food stamps and Medicaid by up to 1%, with no congressional vote required.

The supermajority rule would bar Congress from raising any tax rate or reducing revenues without a three-fifths vote, locking in the new lower rates even if deficits or emergencies later demanded more revenue.
Government and tax-exempt employers would owe a new 20% tax on the value of employee benefits such as health insurance, raising costs for hospitals, universities, and public employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real simplification and a genuine tax cut for middle-income wage earners with children, and its large standard deduction would remove many low earners from the tax rolls. But it is built as a net transfer toward wealth: capital income and inherited estates escape tax entirely while low-income families lose the earned income tax credit and beneficiaries face automatic cuts to Medicare, food assistance, and veterans' benefits to make the numbers balance. The pension provisions — repealing nondiscrimination rules and allowing companies to reclaim surplus pension assets — shift retirement risk from employers onto workers. On balance the design concentrates its gains at the top and pays for them through programs serving ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four committees and then two subcommittees, but no committee ever scheduled action on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Dick Armey, the House Majority Leader, introduced the bill on July 19, 1995, at the height of the Republican majority's push for a flat tax and a balanced budget.
The House referred it to Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, Budget, and Rules, with the Speaker to decide which committee would consider which provisions.
On July 27 it was referred to a Government Reform subcommittee, and on September 5 to a Budget subcommittee on the legislative and budget process — the last recorded action.
Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions, never reported the bill, and no committee or subcommittee held a recorded markup or vote.
The bill had 9 cosponsors, all Republicans, and expired with the Congress on January 3, 1997, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the progressive income tax, the estate tax, and the earned income tax credit survived, workers kept their pension protections, and Medicare, food assistance, and other entitlement programs were spared the automatic cuts the caps would have triggered. High-income households did not receive the untaxed capital income and estate-tax repeal the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Dick Armey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; the chairman was instead advancing his own different tax-overhaul proposal, so the tax provisions never received a markup.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors plus the sponsor were House Republicans, but no floor vote was ever taken and Democrats played no recorded role in the bill's fate; it died quietly in committee.

industries.industry: High-income households and holders of capital
industries.note: The bill would exempt interest, dividends, and capital gains from tax entirely and repeal the estate tax, cutting taxes most for the wealthiest households. The revenue foregone would be made up by taxing wage income and cutting entitlement programs serving ordinary people.

Business income would be taxed at a flat 17–20% with the corporate alternative minimum tax repealed, and employers could withdraw excess pension assets without the 20% excise tax. The offsets come from automatic cuts to Medicare, food assistance, and other benefits ordinary people receive.

industries.industry: Retirees and workers in employer pension plans
industries.note: Repealing pension nondiscrimination, coverage, and top-heavy rules would free employers from maintaining plans that cover lower-paid workers, and letting companies reclaim surplus pension assets without penalty puts workers' retirement security at risk.
A new 20% tax on the value of noncash employee benefits (such as employer health insurance) would raise costs for hospitals, universities, charities, and federal, state, and local governments.

Entitlement spending caps enforced by automatic sequestration could cut Medicare provider payments by up to 4% without a vote of Congress, reducing reimbursement across hospitals and physician practices.
